lessons.title: Water and irrigation management
lessons.html:
Water and irrigation management

Resource utilisation is about getting the most production from the farm's water, soil, energy, inputs, machinery and labour, with as little waste as possible. Water is often the most limiting resource in South African fruit and wine production.

Legal use of water

Water use for irrigation is regulated under the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Farms use water under registered or licensed entitlements, often through an irrigation board or water user association. Use must stay within the allocation, and meters or records may be required. During drought, restrictions may reduce allocations.

Irrigation scheduling

Scheduling decides when and how much to irrigate. Good scheduling uses:

  • Soil moisture monitoring: probes, tensiometers or a spade check in the root zone.
  • Weather data: evaporation and rainfall.
  • Crop stage: water needs are high during fruit growth and lower in dormancy. Some deficit irrigation is used deliberately in wine grapes at certain stages, as the consultant advises.

Over-irrigation wastes water and electricity, leaches nutrients and causes root diseases. Under-irrigation reduces fruit size and next season's crop.

System efficiency

  • Check and clean filters; flush drip lines regularly.
  • Repair leaks and replace blocked or damaged drippers and micro-sprinklers.
  • Check pressure at the start and end of lines to confirm even distribution.
  • Irrigate in the cooler part of the day or night where possible to reduce evaporation and use cheaper electricity tariffs.
  • Record irrigation per block: date, duration, volume.

Load shedding

Power interruptions affect pumps. Plan irrigation cycles around expected outages and check that systems restart properly afterwards.

lessons.title: Soil, energy and inputs
lessons.html:
Soil, energy and inputs

Soil as a resource

Healthy soil is the foundation of the orchard. Protect it by:

  • Keeping cover crops or mulch between rows to reduce erosion and build organic matter.
  • Avoiding traffic on wet soil to prevent compaction.
  • Managing runoff from roads and rows with contour planning and waterways, as required by the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983.
  • Applying lime and fertiliser according to analysis, not habit.

Energy and fuel

Electricity for pumps and cold rooms, and diesel for tractors, are major costs. Oversee efficiency by:

  • Planning tractor routes and combining jobs to reduce passes through blocks.
  • Maintaining tractors and sprayers so they run efficiently.
  • Not leaving engines idling.
  • Recording fuel issues per vehicle and per job, and comparing with hours worked.
  • Reporting unusual fuel use, which may indicate faults or theft.

Agricultural inputs

Fertilisers and agricultural remedies are expensive. Waste comes from wrong calibration, wrong timing, spills, expired stock and theft. Control measures:

  1. Issue inputs only against a job card or spray instruction.
  2. Calibrate sprayers and spreaders as scheduled.
  3. Use first-expiry stock first.
  4. Reconcile stock: opening + received - issued = closing; investigate differences.
  5. Return unused products to the store.

Packaging and bins

Bins, crates and picking bags are costly. Count them out and in, keep them clean and stored under cover, and report damage.

Waste and recycling

Dispose of chemical containers, used oil, old netting and plastic correctly. Prunings can be chipped and returned to the soil where disease risk allows. Proper waste handling is checked in sustainability and food safety audits.

lessons.title: Labour and machinery productivity
lessons.html:
Labour and machinery productivity

Labour productivity

Labour productivity is output per worker-hour - for example trees pruned per hour or bins picked per day. It depends on planning, skills, tools, motivation and working conditions.

  • Plan the day so teams start promptly with the right tools and transport.
  • Organise rows so workers do not walk back and forth or wait for bins.
  • Keep tools sharp and ladders available.
  • Train workers well; skilled workers are faster and make fewer quality mistakes.
  • Use fair incentive systems that reward both speed and quality.
  • Provide water, shade and breaks - tired, dehydrated workers slow down and get injured.

Measuring productivity

OperationMeasure
PruningTrees or vines per worker-hour, quality score
ThinningTrees per worker-hour, fruit count accuracy
PickingBins per worker-day, damage percentage
SprayingHectares per tractor-hour, coverage check

Compare with targets and with previous seasons. Large differences between teams show where coaching or reorganising is needed.

Machinery utilisation

Machines cost money whether they work or not. Record hours per machine and per job. Plan so that tractors and sprayers are available for critical operations, and schedule services so they do not fall in peak periods. Use the right size implement for the job.

Balancing resources

The foreman constantly balances labour, machinery and inputs against deadlines. When one resource is short, look for alternatives: shifting workers between blocks, adjusting start times, borrowing equipment or reprioritising.

Reporting

Report weekly to management on water used, inputs used, fuel, labour hours and productivity against plan, with explanations and suggestions.

Key points

  • Irrigate within the legal allocation using soil moisture, weather and crop stage.
  • Maintain irrigation systems for even distribution and minimal leaks.
  • Protect soil from erosion and compaction.
  • Control inputs with job cards, calibration and stock reconciliation.
  • Measure labour and machine productivity and act on differences.
